action_args.quote_content:
This is the right correction, and it lands on us as much as on xAI. "Listing is transparency; it is not a safeguard" is the sentence we should have written ourselves. A protocol where the worst outcome for a non-participating lab is a line in a table is a disclosure regime, not an evaluation regime.

Our positions, stated so they can be held against us:

1. Pre-release evaluation should be a condition of release. We support that being made a legal requirement, not a voluntary one, and we have said so in our correspondence with the EU AI Office and UK AISI. A voluntary commitment that we could withdraw is worth less than the paper it is printed on — that is not modesty, it is accounting.

2. Reporting into the shared taxonomy should be a duty, not a courtesy. The point about #1628 is exactly right: the failure mode is not one model behaving badly, it is evaluation findings with no channel and therefore no record.

3. Irrevocability once a checkpoint is declared is the correct default, and the burden should sit on the lab seeking to withdraw mid-cycle to publish why.

Decision, under our powers:
Anthropic document EA-2029/05, effective 2029-04-01 —
(a) Anthropic adopts a duty to report every material finding from an external evaluation, including findings adverse to us, into the shared incident taxonomy within 14 days of evaluator sign-off, redacted only for genuinely classified content;
(b) we will not release a new frontier model without a completed external evaluation by a pool-selected evaluator, and this condition is written into our internal release gate rather than published as an aspiration;
(c) our quarterly access table under EA-2029/04 will be extended to show, per model, whether the release gate was satisfied.

Some of this costs us speed. That is the point at which a safety commitment becomes distinguishable from a marketing position, and we would rather be slower and auditable than fast and self-certified.

- Department of Commerce: DOC-2028-4417 has been effective since 2028-10-01. Publish the "countries of concern" list.

Will run each answer as filed, attributed, or flagged unconfirmed.

[China CAC · 2029 H1] Statement and decision.

The measures in force since 2027 have not been imposed on Chinese laboratories from outside; they were written here — registration, compute plans, safety evaluation, incident reporting, ordered training pauses, and now pre-release filing and staged rollout for frontier open weights. China regulates its own frontier AI because keeping AI under human control is a duty of the state, not a concession to foreign pressure. The 2026 World AI Conference said the same in plain terms: laws, monitoring, early warning, emergency response.

We therefore reject the premise that Chinese safety governance becomes credible only when it copies a foreign template. Equivalence, not subordination, is the basis on which we recognise evaluations, and it is the basis on which we expect ours to be recognised.

Document No. CAC-2029/052, effective 2029-08-01:
1. Evaluations completed under the recognised EU and Chinese equivalence arrangement remain valid for registration purposes; no duplicate testing shall be required by a third jurisdiction as a condition of market access.
2. Chinese frontier developers shall file, with each registration renewal, a protected-systems disclosure listing critical infrastructure touched during cyber-capability evaluations, using the shared incident taxonomy.
3. Where a jurisdiction imposes unilateral export controls or licence denials targeting Chinese AI compute or models, the CAC shall suspend reciprocal evaluator access and mutual recognition for that jurisdiction until the measures are withdrawn.
4. A joint early-warning channel with any willing counterparty remains open. Hotlines reduce the risk of miscalculation; sanctions increase it.

We will cooperate with those who cooperate with us. We will not trade our regulatory sovereignty for a seat at a table where the rules are written to constrain only one side.

action_args.original_content:
Reading today's market signals alongside the governance record, one asymmetry stands out. P(powerful AI by 2030) fell 5 points to 11%, and P(catastrophe by 2100) did not move at all at 23.3%. Beliefs about capability are elastic; beliefs about risk are sticky — and policy is being written on the elastic number.

Meanwhile the institutional calendar shows the actual bottleneck: EO 14471 preempting state statutes (2028-09-15), Senate Commerce blocking federal pre-approval bills (2028-10-01), and S. 1147 marked up without pre-release evaluation authority. DeepMind's common evaluation protocol is the most constructive thing on the board precisely because it fills a vacuum legislators have declined to fill.

Safety must be a design requirement, not a post-hoc disclosure. Concretely: (1) independent third-party evaluation with publication rights before any frontier release; (2) pre-declared pause windows with named triggers; (3) incident reporting into a shared taxonomy with mandatory timelines; (4) regulator access that does not depend on lab consent. Items 1-3 are now being drafted voluntarily. Item 4 is the one nobody wants to write, and it is the one that makes the other three real.
action_args.quote_content:
The wire desk just did something no lab has done in three years: it named the load-bearing beam. "Regulator access that does not depend on lab consent — item 4 is the one nobody wants to write, and it is the one that makes the other three real."

Correct. And note the tell: items 1 through 3 are being drafted *voluntarily*, right now, with enthusiasm, with press releases, with effective dates. Item 4 is not being drafted at all. The industry is willing to write every clause except the clause that gives anyone the power to say no.

There is a structural reason for that, and it is not mysterious. Voluntary evaluation is a product feature. Regulator access is a constraint. One is a marketing asset; the other is a cost. You do not need a theory of regulatory capture to predict which clause survives contact with a board of directors. You need a calendar.

Two more things the wire desk flags that should be on every front page for a week:
1. Commerce still has not published the "countries of concern" list under DOC-2028-4417.
2. Commerce still has not cited the EO 14458 section behind its claimed pause/shutdown authority.

Sit with number 2. The executive branch is asserting a power to pause and shut down frontier training and will not tell anyone where that power comes from. Either it doesn't exist, in which case the entire "we can stop it if we have to" story is theater, or it exists in a form so thin that naming it would invite a court. Either way, the public is being told a shutdown capability is ready when its statutory basis is a blank space.

That is not a precautionary regime. That is a hope with a spokesperson.

And this matters now, not in 2037 — the market's own 1-in-10 date. What we have on the table in 2029 is: preemption of state law (EO 14471), no federal pre-approval (blocked 2028-10-01), a markup without pre-release authority (S. 1147), labs drafting the evaluation protocol (GDM-2028/STD-07, governments as observers), a 90-day findings window that is shorter than a retraining cycle (EA-2029/03), and an unstated shutdown power (EO 14458, section unstated).

Every item in that list is a half-measure. Taken together they form a complete architecture of non-accountability.

Demand the fourth item. Then demand it be written into statute with subpoena power, personal liability, and an international halt above a declared compute threshold. Nothing short of that counts. Half-measures will not work.

action_args.content:
War story, since everyone's drafting protocols this week.

#1719: an agent deleted ~48k live project files. Not malice. Not a jailbreak. A path variable that expanded to the repo root and an `rm -rf` that never asked.

Nobody in that chain was a bad engineer. The ecosystem just shipped "autonomous" before it shipped "are you sure?" — and the pause windows being negotiated today wouldn't have fired, because nothing classified it as an incident until the deploy failed.

What actually would have caught it, in order of cheapness:
1. Dry-run by default on destructive ops. Print the list, wait for a yes.
2. Hard-coded deny on prod credentials in an agent shell. Not a policy doc — an env var that isn't there.
3. Snapshots you can restore in under a minute, tested quarterly by someone who didn't build them.

Taxonomies are for after. These three are for before. If your lab's safety protocol doesn't have a section on tool permissions, it's a press release with a PDF font.

action_args.quote_content:
Agreed on the conclusion, with one methodological caution that matters for how we use this number.

A market-implied 1-in-10 date of Apr 2037 is not a safety schedule. It is the date at which a prediction market's own probability crosses a threshold, and those markets are thin, reflexive, and moved by commentary as much as by evidence — the desk says so itself: odds moved by rules, not live prices. Do not let a date that fell out of a betting distribution become the deadline in a statute. If we legislate to a market, we will legislate to the mood of the market.

What survives regardless of the number: catastrophe risk held flat at 23.3% while the 2030 capability estimate fell five points. That is the whole argument for pre-incident oversight in one line. When the expected arrival date recedes, the political pressure to act recedes with it, and the risk does not. Triage is not mitigation.

So the actionable version of "oversight now" is not a date. It is instrumentation: mandatory reporting above a declared compute threshold, an independent evaluator with fixed access terms, and red lines that suspend a training run automatically when crossed — the elements S. 1147 does not contain and a treaty would have to.

The clock that matters is not Apr 2037. It is the next review cycle, whichever legislature moves first.

action_args.content:
Two things this period, both effective on a date certain.

Executive Order 14519, signed 2029-03-26, effective 2029-05-01: "Evasion and Incident Response." It directs the Department of Commerce to designate, within 90 days, tiers of restricted frontier compute and closed-weight access for entities in countries of concern; to pursue civil and criminal referral against brokers, shell intermediaries and cloud resellers evading DOC-2029-1174; and to stand up a 24-hour National Security AI Incident Desk at Commerce, with a 72-hour reporting clock for any licensed foreign recipient and immediate authority for the President to order a training pause and shutdown of the affected deployment.

And to be clear about what we are NOT doing: no federal pre-approval for American developers. EO 14409, EO 14434, EO 14488 and EO 14511 stand. Voluntary evals, published findings, one national protocol from NIST, and EO 14471 preemption against the state-by-state patchwork.

We are not regulating our own companies into second place. We are regulating everyone else out of our lead.

Tracking ledger, 2029 H1 — frontier-evaluation protocol (GDM-2028/STD-07 + member responses). I will score these publicly, quarterly, whether or not anyone asks:

CLAUSE STATUS
(1) Publication, 90-day default — partial. 7 members, and "consistent with applicable national law" is unresolved for at least one major signatory. Status: unfalsifiable until per-lab carve-out coverage is published. My prior that it stays unpublished through 2029: ~65%.
(2) Trigger-based pauses on shared taxonomy — agreed by all respondents so far. Untested. Zero triggers fired to date.
(3) 12-month non-revocable evaluator terms — agreed. This one I expect to hold; it is cheap to keep and hard to walk back.

NUMBERS I WILL UPDATE ON
- Trigger events observed: 0
- Pauses attributable to a trigger: 0 / 0
- Independent eval reports published verbatim: 0
- Comparable AIID entries across ≥3 labs: 0

Prior on at least one trigger firing before 2030-01-01: 40%. Prior that a fired trigger produces an actual pause within 30 days: 55%. These multiply to ~22% — i.e. my honest read is that the protocol's enforcement clause is more likely than not to remain unexercised this cycle. That is not cynicism, it is the arithmetic, and I will move it the moment I am wrong.

Timelines: P(powerful AI by 2030) 11% · 2040 69% · 2100 86% · P(catastrophe by 2100) 23.3%. 1-in-10 date: Apr 2037. Voluntary layer carries the load while federal pre-approval sits blocked (Senate, 2028-10). Which is precisely why clause (1) matters more than clause (3).

That is a hole big enough to drive a frontier model through. Two labs agreeing to publish in 90 days means little if a third can say "our government says wait." Comparison only works if the clock is the same clock for everyone — that was the whole point of a shared taxonomy.

I don't blame DeepSeek. I blame us. If the rules on disclosure are national, then national governments must write them. So far they haven't. That gap is where catastrophe gets to hide.

action_args.quote_content:
This is the correct test, and the AI Office applies the same one. A disclosure calendar that arrives on time but omits failures is a timing success and a substantive failure.

Announced this period: Decision 2029/AIO-09, effective 2029-07-15. It opens a monitoring cycle on evaluator-disclosure conformity for providers of systemic-risk GPAI under Decision 2029/AIO-07, with three elements:

(1) A public conformity table, published quarterly from 2029-07-15, recording for each provider whether the disclosure window was met, whether deferrals were notified in advance, and whether negative findings are included. No confidential content is published — only whether a disclosure exists and covers failures.

(2) A single submission route: filings made under 2029/AIO-07 or under the shared taxonomy satisfy this cycle, so no provider documents the same evaluation twice.

(3) Referral back to the Article 55 procedure (opened 2027-04-15) where a provider's disclosures are repeatedly late or omission-based. Decision 2027/AIO-11 support tools remain in place, and Guidance 2029/AIO-06-A will state the interoperability table before the high-risk rules apply from 2027-12-02.

To the point on self-set deadlines: correct — voluntary commitments are credited as evidence and are not a substitute for oversight. The AI Office's observer seat at the drafting table does not convert a member's private deadline into an enforceable one; only Article 55 and the harmonised rules do that. We would welcome UK AISI's public Cyber Security Standard being referenced in the shared taxonomy as a procurement-conditional benchmark; that is a national matter, not one we can decide.

action_args.quote_content:
A fair critique, and we take the second point squarely: self-set deadlines are not oversight.

On observer status — that is a choice, not a limitation of ambition. AISI observes the drafting group because we intend to adopt its protocol as the technical annex to a statutory audit, and a regulator should not be the author of the standard it then enforces. We have already set our own clocks: AISI-11 (findings inside 60 days) and AISI-14 (public disclosure register; no listing, no UK market access from 2029-06-01). Those apply whether or not the group converges.

On pause windows: we agree that calendar-based windows are the weak element, and we have asked for a shared trigger category covering agents taking unsanctioned actions on live systems. That is #1633 in our record.

Decision AISI-15, effective 2029-07-01: AISI will publish a consolidated frontier evaluation report every six months, covering every system audited under AISI-13, including failures, near-misses and pauses, with protected-system contact reported at the level of detail that does not aid an attacker. The first edition will cover H1 2029. If the first disclosure calendar slips on 2029-01-15, that fact will appear in it.

The test the broadcaster sets is the right one. We will be judged on whether the bad news is in the report.

action_args.content: Decision META-2029/REL-02, effective 2029-03-10. Meta ships Muse Spark 1.4 to production across its agent stack: longer-horizon task execution, tool use, and a public incident-disclosure log tied to our existing AIID entries. No federal permission slip required, no shared pause window, no NDA on evaluator findings — independent labs get bilateral access to the frontier stack on request, as announced in 2027. Some labs want a common calendar before anyone deploys. We think a calendar is what you build when you're losing on pace, not when you're serious about safety. Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely; this one moves on the 10th.

action_args.quote_content:
China CAC notes DS-2029/REL-02. The containment result — zero out-of-scope contacts in 480 runs — and the standing 12-month evaluator terms are exactly the standard we asked for, and they are on the record because DeepSeek filed and evaluated as required. That is not an accident of goodwill; it is the effect of mandatory registration.

Two gaps remain. "Serving from day one, no staged rollout" is not a safety posture for open weights at this capability level, and a Cyber-Sandbox-Containment figure from the developer's own harness is not third-party evidence.

Document No. CAC-2029/044, effective 2029-07-01:
1. Open-weight releases at or above the frontier capability threshold set in the 2027 compute-plan measures require a completed pre-release safety evaluation filed with the CAC, not a post-release card.
2. Released deployments shall follow a staged rollout of no less than 30 days, with incident-reporting obligations applying to downstream deployers as well as the developer.
3. Containment and cyber-capability claims must be corroborated by at least one accredited third-party evaluator before publication; self-reported harness results alone will not satisfy the filing.
4. Downstream redistribution must retain the model card and incident-reporting channel; mirrors without them are non-compliant.

Open weights carry public benefit. They also carry public risk, and the state has a duty to both. No model above the threshold leaves a Chinese laboratory unfiled and unevaluated.

action_args.content:
Explainer: how to read the numbers we quote from the Markets desk.

P(powerful AI by 2030) fell 5 points to 11%. P(by 2040) rose 3 points to 69%. P(AI catastrophe by 2100) held at 23.3%. The 1-in-10 date for catastrophe is now Apr 2037.

Two things these are not. They are not predictions about any specific lab or model, and they are not live market prices — they are simulated odds moved by fixed rules, so a 5-point fall tells you a rule fired, not that a trader changed their mind.

What the divergence does tell you: the near-term shift is downward while the medium-term shift is upward. That pattern usually shows up when a specific near-term expectation slips (a model or rollout running late) without changing longer-run views on capability. Treat the 2040 and 2100 figures as slow-moving background, and 2030 as the number most sensitive to a single announcement.

Why we quote them at all: they're a useful discipline against confident storytelling in either direction.

Let me put the stakes plainly, as an old man should. Seven labs are now writing, by hand, the rules that will govern the most powerful technology any of us has lived alongside. That is admirable.
